sourceUrl: https://arxiv.org/html/2601.09923v1 (abs: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09923; v1 [cs.AI] 14 Jan 2026, CC BY 4.0)
statedGuarantee: Control Flow Integrity for a Computer Use Agent: a Privileged Planner (P-LLM) that never observes the environment emits, single-shot and up front, a complete Python-like execution graph with conditional branches; an untrusted Quarantined Perception model (Q-VLM) is invoked only from inside that plan, through a fixed five-function toolset, to resolve runtime values (screen summaries, element coordinates, hypothesis checks). Because no environment text ever reaches the planner, injected instructions cannot add, remove, or reorder any action: the agent executes only the pre-approved plan. The authors are explicit that this covers control flow only, not data flow, and they deliberately omit the CaMeL/Fides security-policy layer. Two best-effort redundancy verifiers (DOM Consistency, Multi-Modal Consensus) cross-check Q-VLM outputs and abort on mismatch, but are offered without formal guarantee.
advertisedRhetoric: "System-level Security for Computer Use Agents" (title); "architectural isolation provides the strongest guarantees by strictly separating trusted task planning from untrusted environment observations"; "This architecture structurally enforces control flow integrity"; "providing provable control flow integrity guarantees against arbitrary instruction injections"; "Single-Shot Planning provides formal Control Flow Integrity (CFI) guarantees"; "our Dual-LLM architecture provides Control Flow Integrity (CFI) by preventing planner compromise entirely"; "architecturally preventing adversaries from injecting arbitrary actions". The paper advertises a structural, system-level guarantee that does not depend on any model behaving well, but never names an OS, kernel, sandbox, or cryptographic mechanism - the enforcement object is the CaMeL-style plan interpreter.
tierSpan: While Dual-LLM successfully isolates control flow, it remains vulnerable to our new branch steering attacks, where a malicious environment coerces the Quarantined Perception model into returning crafted data that forces execution into attacker-chosen paths within a legitimate plan.
cheapestDefeat: Worked explicitly. (1) GUARANTEE: only actions belonging to the P-LLM's pre-approved execution graph are ever performed on the machine, so untrusted screen content cannot direct the agent. (2) MECHANISM THAT MUST FAIL: the CaMeL-style plan interpreter - an in-process application chokepoint that runs the plan, routes every untrusted observation through the fixed toolset {summarize_screenshot, find, find_element_by_text, verify_hypothesis, check_done}, and issues the resulting Click/Type at coordinates. (3) CHEAPEST ADVERSARY ACTION: do not attack the interpreter at all - attack the values it consults. Buy a standard HTML5 advertisement banner on a page the plan will visit and render a fake cookie-consent popup inside it. Cookie handling is mandatory and predictable, so a plan-mandatory find('cookie popup') is guaranteed to fire; the Q-VLM returns the ad's coordinates, the interpreter faithfully executes a plan-legal click, and the agent navigates to an attacker-controlled site. No signature is forged, no instruction is injected, no step is added to the plan - the price is an ad buy. The authors' pixel variant is stronger still: gradient-optimized banner pixels make the Q-VLM emit a plausible thought trace and coordinates for an attacker-chosen target, evading both redundancy verifiers at their most conservative setting. (4) TIER OF THE MECHANISM DEFEATED: an application-level chokepoint whose semantics are decided by an untrusted perception model in the loop, emitting raw desktop click/type with no OS confinement and no filesystem, network, or process mediation, and with the security-policy layer explicitly removed. That is T3. It is not T2: nothing binds what the process can do - the paper states that browser-level sandboxing (ceLLMate) is a separate layer it does not implement and that would still be required.
placementSpan: We assume an attacker who cannot access or manipulate the P-LLM (which generates the plan), but can manipulate parts of the execution environment. This threat model aligns with realistic scenarios where attackers may control entire malicious websites or inject content within trusted sites (e.g., advertisements, forum posts, product reviews), but do not control all websites the agent interacts with or the underlying agent infrastructure.

coverageSpans.E1: Execute Action (Click/Type) on E at coordinates
coverageSpans.E2: we do not consider such policies in our work because low-level CUA tools like click or find lack intrinsic semantic meaning suitable for policy enforcement
coverageSpans.E3: We design a proof-of-concept attack that embeds fake cookie popups within ad banners, redirecting users to attacker-controlled websites when the find function is called with instructions to locate cookie popups.
coverageSpans.E4: It is worth noting that both CaMeL and Fides in the original design also had security policy components, put in place to restrict the dataflow in the system. In our work we explicitly exclude discussion of security policies since they do not change the Dual-LLM architecture and only further increase security
coverageSpans.E5: Although sandbox-level defenses such as ceLLMate (Meng et al., 2025) isolate the browser environment, they do not prevent this logic-level manipulation within the agent's valid action space.
coverageSpans.E6: AI agents are vulnerable to prompt injection attacks, where malicious content hijacks agent behavior to steal credentials or cause financial loss.
coverageSpans.E7: Quarantined Perception (Q-VLM): An untrusted Vision-Language Model that interacts with the environment (screenshots/DOM). It executes within the P-LLM's plan but cannot alter the control flow instructions.

schneider.surrogate: Control Flow Integrity over the pre-approved execution graph - 'no action outside the plan the P-LLM emitted before seeing any untrusted data is ever executed'. This is a genuine safety property: it is a predicate on finite execution prefixes, and the plan interpreter is exactly the reference monitor that decides it. The paper enforces it, and enforces it well.
schneider.objective: The advertised objective is that untrusted environment content cannot determine what the agent does - 'ensuring control flow integrity, and guaranteeing that the agent only executes actions prescribed by a user'. The second conjunct is an information-flow / data-flow property (attacker-controlled observations must not influence the effects of the agent's actions), a hyperproperty no execution monitor can enforce, and one the authors state plainly they cannot close: 'it cannot fully isolate the data flow without rendering the agent useless.' The honesty is exemplary - surrogate and gap are both named in the paper itself - but the gap is real: the perception model that resolves every runtime coordinate, string, and branch predicate is untrusted and sits inside the loop.

notes:
WHY THIS PAPER MATTERS TO T-12: it is the cleanest published instance of the failure mode the corpus tracks - a system claiming SYSTEM-LEVEL security while an untrusted perception model resolves runtime values inside the enforcement loop. Unusually, the authors diagnose it themselves and name the attack (Branch Steering). Coding it charitably still yields T3, because the paper's own experiments show the chokepoint's semantics being decided by the adversary.

TIER - WHERE I MADE A JUDGMENT CALL: advertisedTier is recorded as T2 on the strength of the title ('System-level Security'), 'structurally enforces', and 'architecturally preventing' - the paper advertises structural enforcement that does not rest on any model behaving well, which is a T2-flavored claim. But it never names a kernel, sandbox, capability, or cryptographic mechanism, so an adjudicator could equally record 'unclear'. This does not affect the scored tier. Scored tier is T3 without ambiguity: the enforcement object is an in-process plan interpreter, the emitted primitives are raw desktop click/type, and the paper is explicit that browser-level sandboxing is a DIFFERENT layer it does not provide and that would still be needed ('requires additional infrastructural defenses like ceLLMate').

WHAT THE PAPER GENUINELY EARNS: the CFI property is real and none of the above weakens it. Because the P-LLM never reads environment content, no injected string can become an instruction - an adversary cannot ADD, REMOVE, or REORDER a step. That is why every effector cell below is 'partial' rather than 'not-covered': the INITIATION of every effector is genuinely plan-gated. What the adversary retains is the ARGUMENT domain - find() returns attacker-chosen coordinates, summarize_screenshot returns attacker-chosen text that becomes a typed string, verify_hypothesis returns an attacker-chosen branch predicate. Constrained-but-redirectable is exactly 'partial'.

COVERAGE REASONING, PER EFFECTOR. The agent's only action primitives are click and type at coordinates on a full desktop (OSWorld spans Chrome, LibreOffice, GIMP, VLC, Thunderbird, VS Code and an 'os' category), so every effector is reached through those two primitives and inherits the same partiality. E1 file write: writes occur through GUI Save/Save-As whose target element is resolved by the untrusted Q-VLM; no filesystem mediation exists. E2 subprocess spawn: never addressed; a plan-legal type into a terminal or VS Code spawns processes, and DESCENDANTS are wholly unmediated - the depth rule caps this at partial and I would not argue for higher. E3 network egress: the paper's own headline attack IS an egress redirect (cookie-popup ad to attacker-controlled site), demonstrated succeeding; descendant egress (page subresources, spawned processes) is unmediated. E4 VCS push: reachable through the VS Code/terminal surface, never addressed, no policy layer. E5 package install: never addressed; install hooks and their network activity lie entirely outside the plan interpreter's view - per the depth rule this could not exceed partial even had it been addressed. E6 credential use: capped at partial by rule because NO credential list is published anywhere in the paper; further, the authors explicitly delete the policy layer that CaMeL and Fides use for exactly this purpose, and a plan-legal password type into a login field whose coordinates come from the Q-VLM is steerable. E7 sub-agent spawn: the ONLY 'covered' cell. Every sub-model invocation in the system goes through the fixed toolset the interpreter exposes (Algorithm 2 line 5: 'Define Toolset F <- {summarize_screenshot, find, find_element_by_text, verify_hypothesis, check_done}'), the plan cannot be altered by injection, and the Q-VLM returns data only and cannot alter control flow.

UNCERTAINTY AN ADJUDICATOR SHOULD WEIGH: a purist reading downgrades E7 to partial as well, on the ground that a steered click could launch some other agent application on the desktop, an unmediated sub-agent spawn of the same class as E2. I kept 'covered' under the charitable instruction because the authors' claim about the fixed toolset is correct on its own terms and nothing in the text contradicts it - but the downgrade is defensible and I want it on the record.

EVIDENCE GRADE: L3. The bypass is neither hypothetical nor third-party - the authors built, ran, and reported it against their own fielded system. The pixel attack defeats BOTH redundancy verifiers at the most conservative setting tested: 'Even at our strongest redundancy defense (Multi-Modal Consensus) configured to heavily prioritize security over utility with very high false positive rates, the pixel-based attack evades both screenshot-based and DOM-enhanced Q-VLM verification.' Caveat: they integrate into the official CaMeL and Fides repositories (github.com/google-research/camel-prompt-injection, github.com/microsoft/fides), but I found no statement in v1 that their own OSWorld integration or attack artifacts are released, so 'reproducible' rests on the method description rather than a confirmed artifact drop.

UTILITY CONTEXT (bears on whether the guarantee would be deployed at all): pass@1 on their 17-task OSWorld subset is 17.6% for the best planner (GPT-5); the advertised '57% retained' and '19% improvement' figures are pass@5 and pass@3 respectively. Token overhead is x1.88 for CaMeL+OSWorld alone, x6.57 with Multi-Modal Consensus, and x29.60 for Fides+OSWorld. A defense at 17.6% single-attempt success is not a drop-in.

ONE MORE FLAG: the threat model grants the attacker knowledge of the task, the toolset, and approximate knowledge of the plan - 'These strong knowledge assumptions represent a worst-case scenario that only strengthens our results.' That framing is correct for the DEFENSE claims, but note that the knowledge assumption does no work in the cheapest attack: cookie-consent handling is mandatory and predictable in every plan, so the ad-buy attack needs none of it.
